findings.claim: validate_claude_token's docstring promises 'False for anything else, including a host this probe could not reach — "could not tell" is not a pass', but the implementation returns True for every HTTPError code other than literally 401 or 403. A 500/502/529 (server error / overloaded) from the upstream is exactly a 'could not tell' outcome — it says nothing about the credential — yet it is reported as a valid, authenticated token. This is the same class of silent-success-on-indeterminate-result that Appendix J measured for the code this function exists to replace, just moved one level down.

check_readiness catches every git_mirror.GitError from export_saffron_dir and treats it identically to 'no .saffron at this base_sha', silently setting exported = None. But GitError is also raised by export_saffron_dir for genuine failures unrelated to absence — a bad archive invocation, a corrupted mirror, or a tar that fails to extract — and none of those get distinguished from the ordinary 'repo hasn't onboarded yet' case. The precedent this comment cites (cli._protected_paths_at) explicitly relies on a second, unguarded export_saffron_dir call later in the pipeline to catch a genuinely broken mirror; check_readiness is itself meant to be that authoritative once-per-run gate, so masking a real export failure here means a broken run can be reported ok=True instead of failing readiness with a nameable reason.

The entire point of `validate_claude_token` — per its own docstring and Appendix J — is that it must return `False` when the upstream answers 401/403 (the opposite verdict from `assert_proxy_reaches_upstream`, which treats 401 as a pass on the same host). No test in this diff ever exercises that branch: `test_a_present_but_invalid_token_fails_readiness` injects a fake `validate_token=lambda token: False` that bypasses the real function entirely, and `test_the_token_probes_default_request_shape_is_asserted_not_sent` only forces a `urllib.error.URLError` (a different except clause) to assert the request shape, never an `HTTPError`. Changing line 315 from `return exc.code not in (401, 403)` to `return True` — silently inverting the one behaviour this whole spec exists to add, so an expired token would again pass — leaves all 1264+ tests green.
